newsitem.title: USA: Two auction houses plan sale of rocks from Mars.
newsitem.headline: Two auction houses plan sale of rocks from Mars.

text.p: Barely two months after scientists revealed evidence of possible ancient life on Mars, two New York auction houses have set plans to sell fragments of meteorites from the red planet.

One of the auction houses, Guernsey's, estimated that three fragments that weigh about one pound in total would sell for up to $2 million, which would make Mars rocks worth much more than ever before.

That should not be surprising, after scientists from NASA and Stanford University said in August they had found evidence of single-cell life on Mars in remains from a meteorite that fell to Earth about 13,000 years ago.
Guernsey's said the rocks, one of which is similar to the one that the scientists examined for their discovery, are being sold by a private collector whom the auction house would not identify.
Where did the collector get the rocks?
From museums, according to Arlan Ettinger, who founded Guernsey's with his wife 20 years ago. Over the years the man traded with museums, a common practice among collectors, Ettinger said.
He also said it was the right time to sell the items, given the big news announced over the summer.
"Nothing major from Mars was sold before and this is certainly the first (sale) since the August announcement," he said in an interview.

Scientists hailed the announcement as one of the major discoveries of the century, if not the millenium. The story made front-page news around the world. Religious leaders said it could have vast implications on human thought.
Still, other scientists noted the evidence was far from conclusive and some cautioned against spending billions of dollars on missions to Mars.

Enter Guernsey's. The auction house, younger but sometimes more nimble than its competitors, Christie's and Sotheby's, quickly set its sights on landing the meteorite collection once word about the seller's wishes started circulating.
"It meant a great deal to us," Ettinger said. Not only because of the competition, but because "we've gotten something good that I'm proud to present."
Separately, Phillips auction house plans to sell three fragments of meteorites from Mars in New York as part of a natural history auction on Dec. 14.
Aside from its origins, the collection being auctioned by Guernsey's is noteworthy because it contains all three known types of Martian meteorites, Ettinger said.

Each type is named for where it was first discovered: Shergottite (Shergotty, India), Nakhlite (Nakhla, Egypt) and Chassignite (Chassigny, France). The Shergottite fragment being sold by Guernsey's was actually part of meteorite found in Zagami, Nigeria.
Guernsey's considers its combination of items so unusual that the three fragments are the only lot for sale at its Nov. 20 auction. Auctions typically feature hundreds or thousands of lots.

Mars rock, of course, is extremely rare. Just 90 pounds are known to exist on Earth, according to experts consulted by Guernsey's. All but eight pounds are owned by museums. By contrast, there are about 800 pounds of moon rocks on Earth.
The size of the meteorites being sold is also impressive by Mars rock standards, Ettinger said.
The smallest weighs about 13.5 grams, or half an ounce, slightly smaller than a golf ball, and the largest is 420 grams, or almost a pound.

Phillips plans to sell three fragments weighing between 1.5 grams and 14 grams, said David Herskowitz, a natural history expert at the New York auction house. Herskowitz expects the fragments to fetch as much as $2,000 a gram.
At $2 million, the 498.5 grams that Guernsey's is selling would be worth about $4,000 apiece, well above the $500 to $1,000 a gram that Mars rocks have fetched in the past, collectors said.

Darryl Pitt, a music executive who is curator for a large, private meteorite collection, said after NASA's August announcement that prices had jumped to about $2,000 a gram for Zagami meteorites, but that they could be found for less.
Ettinger said part of the proceeds from the Guernsey's auction will be donated to the American Cancer Society.
Public previews for the Guernsey's sale will be held Nov. 19-20. A 56-page catalogue is available for $25. Call 212 794-2280 or fax 212 744-3638.
A $22 catalogue for the Phillips auction is due next month. Call 212 570-4830 or 800 825-2781.
